replies.text: I'll have to dig out the stamps and get back to you on that. I'm also curious about the value of my 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle baseball card. Do you know how rare it is and what it's worth?
replies.reply:
The 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle is arguably the most famous postwar baseball card, but a quick heads-up: it's not actually rare in the usual sense — Topps printed a lot of them, and high-grade examples aren't scarce because of mass finds. What drives the price is condition, brutally so.

Rough market picture (as of my knowledge, and prices move around):

- Heavily worn/creased or trimmed: a few hundred dollars, sometimes less
- Mid-grade (PSA 3–5): roughly $5,000–$40,000
- High grade (PSA 6–8): six figures ($100k–$500k+)
- PSA 9s and the fabled "Mantle 10s": $1M to $10M+

So the honest answer is: rarity isn't really the question — your card's grade is everything. Centering, corners, edges, surface, and whether it's original (there are convincing alterations and reprints out there). Your first step should be getting it graded by PSA or SGC; that costs a bit but transforms what you can actually sell it for. Also check the green color under the cap and the back — reprint red flags are worth ruling out before you get hopeful.

And yes, going back to the other thread: whenever you dig out those Eastern European stamps, I'm still keen to see the countries, dates, and denominations so we can narrow down what's worth something.

replies.text: I'm also thinking of getting back into vintage toy collecting, specifically G.I. Joe action figures. Do you know anything about the rarity and value of vintage G.I. Joe figures from the 1960s? I recently acquired one that's in near-mint condition and I'm curious about its worth.
replies.reply:
1960s G.I. Joe is a different market from the 3¾-inch figures most people picture — the originals were 12-inch, cardboard-boxed "action soldiers," and condition matters to an almost brutal degree. A truly near-mint figure with an unblemished box and complete accessories can run from a few hundred dollars for common Nurse GI Joe or African-American variants aside — the scarcest ones — into the low thousands, especially if the box, insert, and paperwork survive. Sealed examples or rare variants (the Nurse, foreign-market releases) go higher.

The big value shifter is the box: complete, uncrushed boxes can be worth more than the figure itself. Also check whether the paint on the fuzzy hair is intact — head paint wear is the most common flaw.

To size yours up, tell me which release it is (Action Soldier, Sailor, Marine, Pilot), the box markings and copyright date, whether it has its original accessories, and the box condition. Then cross-check eBay *sold* listings — asking prices lie; sold prices don't — and the GI Joe groups/price guides devoted to the twelve-inch era.

And I'll admit I'm getting a pattern here: the Mantle card, the Eastern European stamps, now Joe — you're collecting the collections. How did this one land in your hands?

replies.text: I'm also curious about the Pokémon booster pack I got on eBay. Do you know how rare the cards are in a 1995 Pokémon Trading Card Game booster pack?
replies.reply:
Ha — your collection research keeps branching: stamps, Mantle card, G.I. Joe, now Pokémon. I love it.

A real 1995 booster pack is a bit of a catch, because Wizards of the Coast only began printing the English Base Set in early 1999. So a pack stamped "1995" is almost certainly either a Japanese pack (some early Japanese print runs and promo materials carry earlier dates), a reprinted/reissued pack, or a fan-made/art piece. Worth checking the copyright line on the wrapper and the symbol on the cards.

Rarity-wise in a genuine Base Set booster (11 cards): mostly commons and uncommons, with a rare in every pack. Of those rares, roughly one in three was upgraded to a holo — that's where Charizard lives, at about 1 in every 8–9 packs, and even then often in rough shape from soft 90s printing. So pulling a PSA-worthy Charizard from an old pack is genuinely rare, but a clean rare like Blastoise or Alakaraza... Alakazam still has decent value.

Quick caveat: sealed reprints and fakes are common on eBay, so real money only changes hands if the wrapper itself checks out. What does the wrapper actually say on it — "1995" in a copyright line, or something else?

replies.text: I'm thinking of displaying my new Pokémon booster pack in a special case to preserve its condition. Do you know any good ways to store and display collectible items like this?
replies.reply:
Fun pivot — and honestly, storing it properly is smart regardless of whether that "1995" pack turns out to be Japanese, a reprint, or something fake. Here's what works for packs:

**Long-term protection**
- Acrylic booster-pack display cases (Ultra PRO makes a good one) — rigid, UV-resistant, sized to the pack
- Keep it out of direct sunlight; UV fades wrapper ink, and humidity warps it
- Gravity-feed or stand-up display stands work if you don't want a full case
- Store flat or standing in a cool, dry spot — attics and basements will ruin wrappers

**If you think it's valuable**
- Grading through PSA or CGC encapsulates and seals the pack with a grade — that's the gold standard for high-value sealed product, though it means no casual display access
- If it's sentimental but likely not valuable, the acrylic case alone is the right call — cheaper and looks sharp on a shelf

**One caution:** don't open it "to check the cards," since sealed packs (even questionable ones) usually hold more value sealed — and if it really is misprinted as 1995, the wrapper itself is the interesting artifact.

Before you invest in an expensive case, I'd still verify what the wrapper actually says — that cheap acrylic display looks just as nice either way, but you'd store a genuine Base Set pack differently than a curiosity piece. What does the copyright line on it read?
